questions.question: True or false: Nechama Leibowitz was born in Riga, Latvia.
questions.explanation: She was born in 1905 and grew up in a rich intellectual environment.

questions.question: In which year did Nechama Leibowitz immigrate to the Land of Israel?
questions.explanation: At the age of 25 she settled in Jerusalem and devoted her life to teaching Torah, Prophets and Writings.

questions.question: At which universities in Germany did she study?
questions.explanation: Her higher academic education enabled her to bridge the philological world and the world of Torah.

questions.question: True or false: Nechama Leibowitz adopted the methods of biblical criticism.
questions.explanation: She rejected them completely, and saw in them "an attempt to take from the people of Israel what is theirs."

questions.question: What were the "gilyonot" (study sheets) that she distributed from 1942?
options: Weekly question sheets on the weekly Torah portion, which the learners answered in writing
Booklets of halakha for the festivals
questions.explanation: They were born of envelopes of questions that she sent to students who felt that they had not learned enough from her, and became an enterprise for thousands of learners.

questions.question: Which question is the symbol of her method?
questions.explanation: The assumption: Rashi brings a homily or an explanation only in order to resolve a genuine difficulty in the plain meaning of Scripture.

questions.question: True or false: Leibowitz liked to give lectures to an audience that came only to listen.
questions.explanation: She rejected the "lecture" completely, and demanded that the learners be active and discover the Torah for themselves.

questions.question: What did Leibowitz demand of her students in class?
options: To arrive on time and to come with a Tanakh
To sit quietly and take notes
questions.explanation: At the beginning of each series of lessons she asked her students about their residence and occupations, in order to create a warm space of discourse.

questions.question: What did she reply to Rabbi Yoel Bin-Nun, who claimed that she has no direct reading of Scripture?
options: "The plain meaning is what I understand"
"If you read without commentaries, then you are the commentator, and are you better than all the commentators?!"
"There is no need for commentators in our generation"
questions.explanation: A reading detached from the great commentators seemed to her arrogance, and even impudence.

questions.question: True or false: Leibowitz's personal archive was deposited in the National Library.
questions.explanation: It was deposited in September 2021, and opened a window onto the study of her methods and her letters.

questions.question: What did Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook say when he was asked whether she could be invited to teach at the yeshiva?
options: "It is forbidden to teach at a yeshiva"
"Nechama, certainly it is possible; she is a talmidat chakham"
questions.explanation: The recognition of her as a "talmidat chakham" (a female Torah scholar) crossed sectors.

questions.question: Who, according to his daughter's testimony, listened to her lessons on the radio during meals?
questions.explanation: Adina Bar-Shalom related that her father urged her to learn from her and from her ways.

questions.question: True or false: Leibowitz regarded herself as a feminist and supported women putting on tefillin.
questions.explanation: She rejected the feminist label and a declarative halakhic change.

questions.question: How did she explain why she does not put on tefillin?
options: In a free moment it is better to visit a sick person, a commandment that she is obligated in
Because she has no time to learn
Because her brother instructed her so
questions.explanation: Religious value in her eyes is measured by practical commitment, and not by adopting commandments that one is not commanded in.

questions.question: Who was her brother, who was also a prominent thinker?
questions.explanation: The esteem between them was mutual, but she strongly objected to some of his political statements.

questions.question: True or false: Nechama Leibowitz died in Jerusalem at the age of 92.
questions.explanation: In 1997. On the 100th anniversary of her birth an international conference was held in her memory in New York and in Tel Aviv.

questions.question: What did Leibowitz claim about the relationship between derash (homiletic interpretation) and peshat (plain meaning), according to the research?
options: Derash is detached from the text
Derash reveals "the depth of the plain meaning of Scripture"
Derash is meant for children only
questions.explanation: She used philology to show that the Sages and the Rishonim were sensitive to every double expression and grammatical deviation.

questions.question: Why did she regard Benno Jacob, a Reform commentator, as an important source?
options: Because he was an Orthodox Torah scholar
Because he translated the Bible into German
Because he agreed with biblical criticism
His arguments against biblical criticism were the best ever written
questions.explanation: She said that she learned from his books more than from the books of devout and wholehearted people, because they opened her eyes to "the Torah in its truth."

questions.question: What did Prof. Ephraim Elimelech Urbach say about Nechama Leibowitz?
options: That she is the only one in our generation worthy of writing a new commentary on the Torah
That she is greater than her brother Yeshayahu
That she should be granted semikha (rabbinic ordination)
That she is the great researcher of biblical criticism
questions.explanation: In this way she was recognized as a Torah authority in the academic world as well.

questions.question: How did the gilyonot become a tool for building identity, according to the research?
options: They were given as a prize to outstanding students
The learner answered in writing and was corrected personally, and felt that the Torah is his and that his voice is heard
They were mandatory in all schools
questions.explanation: She read, corrected and returned thousands of sheets, and turned one-directional knowledge into an active discourse.
